content: In 2019, a study was conducted to analyze the return of HIV-positive test results to individuals within a calendar year. The concept of treatment-adjusted prevalence was introduced, which refers to the estimated national HIV prevalence after excluding individuals on antiretroviral therapy (ART) from both the numerator and denominator. This adjusted prevalence includes undiagnosed individuals with HIV, those aware of their status but not on treatment, and those who initiated treatment but later disengaged from care. Rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) for HIV are widely used due to their simplicity and ease of storage. These tests allow trained lay providers to establish an HIV diagnosis during a single visit in community or healthcare settings. However, in some cases, additional laboratory testing, such as Western blotting, is required to confirm a positive diagnosis. Delays in returning results from laboratory testing can hinder ART initiation and result in loss to follow-up. To improve access to underserved populations, innovative testing approaches like self-testing and triage testing are recommended alongside standard testing methods. These approaches often provide same-day results, facilitating rapid initiation of ART. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes the importance of accurate diagnosis, as false-negative results can delay treatment and increase the risk of HIV transmission, while false-positive results can lead to unnecessary lifelong treatment and significant psychosocial, ethical, and legal consequences. The accuracy of HIV testing depends on the testing strategy and algorithm used. WHO recommends following standardized testing strategies and verifying algorithms to minimize discrepancies and misdiagnoses. However, some programs deviate from WHO guidelines, such as using a single reactive test for diagnosis or applying strategies designed for high-prevalence settings in low-prevalence areas. These deviations can undermine confidence in health systems and waste limited resources. Testing strategies involve a sequence of tests to achieve specific objectives, such as infection screening or diagnosis. When specific products are incorporated into a strategy, it becomes a testing algorithm. WHO recommends using a combination of RDTs and enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) to achieve a positive predictive value (PPV) of at least 99%, ensuring accurate diagnoses even in low-prevalence settings. In response to changes in the HIV epidemic, WHO now advises high-burden countries to adopt a strategy of three consecutive reactive test results to confirm an HIV-positive diagnosis. This approach ensures accurate diagnoses as national HIV testing services (HTS) positivity rates decline. Countries with HTS positivity above 5% may continue using two reactive tests but should monitor positivity rates and transition to the three-test strategy when rates fall below 5%. In Malawi, the number of adults living with HIV has increased due to longer lifespans on ART. However, the proportion of undiagnosed individuals has declined significantly, from 78% in 2005 to 14% in 2017, and is projected to reach 6% by 2025. This shift has led to a decrease in HTS positivity and new HIV-positive diagnoses. Despite a doubling in the number of people tested between 2015 and 2017, HTS positivity decreased by 50%, and new diagnoses have continued to decline since 2016. As HTS positivity declines, the PPV of the current two-test strategy in Malawi will drop below 97% by 2025, even if tests meet WHO prequalification standards. To address this, the adoption of a three-test strategy is recommended. This change will require fewer additional tests compared to the current strategy, optimizing resource use while maintaining diagnostic accuracy. WHO's updated guidelines emphasize the importance of adapting testing strategies to the evolving HIV epidemic. By adopting the three-test strategy, countries can ensure accurate diagnoses and maintain confidence in their health systems as HTS positivity rates continue to decline globally.
